keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (no Cliopatria row). The page gives no area; the Yaroslavl oblast (about 39,000 km2) plus Lake Kubenskoye and the Sheksna is my reading of the rivers it lists (the Mologa has no gazetteer entry). Cliopatria draws these lands as Rostov-Suzdal to 1240, nothing 1241-1293, and Vladimir-Suzdal from 1294; its Vladimir-Suzdal shapes of 1422-1462 are this land (see the principality-of-vladimir-suzdal notes), so the renderer must give them to this state. Corrected 2026-11-01 after the review: the Yaroslavl-oblast proxy had covered the seats of three other principalities, so discs round Rostov Veliky (40 km), Uglich (30 km) and Pereslavl-Zalessky (30 km, coordinates 56.733 N 38.850 E from its page) are cut out; the oblast's southern part belongs to Rostov, Uglich and Moscow, not to Yaroslavl. The Yaroslavl page names only Yaroslavl itself and says the principality came 'from the Principality of Rostov'; it does not mention Uglich or Pereslavl. Rostov: the Ivan III page lists 'the Principality of Yaroslavl in 1463, Rostov in 1474, Tver in 1485' as separate absorptions. Uglich: 'From 1218 until 1328, Uglich was the seat of a small princedom' whose princes 'sold their rights to the great prince of Moscow', and Ivan III 'gave the town in 1462 to his younger brother Andrey Bolshoy' (Uglich page). Pereslavl: 'Between 1175 and 1302, Pereslavl was the seat of a principality; in 1302, it was inherited by the prince of Moscow' (Pereslavl-Zalessky page). The remaining shape (172 cells, about 43,500 km2 against 53,100 km2 before) is still a reading: the discs are rough, the Mologa has no gazetteer entry, and the oblast edge is not the principality's border.

ledger.note: 1218: Vsevolod Konstantinovich becomes the first prince of Yaroslavl. The infobox gives 'Established: 1218' and the princes list 'Vsevolod Konstantinovich (r. 1218 - 1238)'; it 'separated from Vladimir-Suzdal when the sons of Konstantin Vsevolodovich divided his lands upon his death' (Konstantin died in 1218; the Vladimir-Suzdal page has Konstantin dividing the lands between 'his brothers' after 1216, a disagreement between the pages).

ledger.note: 1463: Yaroslavl passes to Moscow. The principality 'existed from 1218 until 1463 (de jure until 1471)' and became part of the Grand Duchy of Moscow; the last prince, Aleksandr Bryukhaty, was forced to sign away the succession to Ivan III (page, paraphrased) (no year given).

wars.name: Mongol invasion of Rus (Yaroslavl, 1238)
wars.outcome: Battle of the Sit River, 4 March 1238: Vsevolod Konstantinovich killed. The page records no change of border; a rising against Mongol tribute collectors followed in 1262.
wars.note: Konstantin was killed at Tugova Gora on 3 July 1257. In 1332 Ivan I of Moscow burnt Yaroslavl 'under the Khan's orders' and forced Vasily Davidovich to marry his daughter; the Khan then told Vasily to 'stay loyal to Moscow'.

notes: New state flagged by eu-16-g (the 1422-1462 Vladimir-Suzdal shapes). Two pages (page budget: no Cliopatria shape). The Yaroslavl article is a stub with no area. The Wikipedia title 'Principality of Rostov' redirects to Vladimir-Suzdal and 'Principality of Uglich' is the town article, so Rostov (1207-1474) and Uglich do not get their own dossiers (no article of their own): their lands remain blank after 1389 in the Vladimir-Suzdal dossier and need a gap-filler decision (extend the Moscow dossier, or add them from the Ivan III page). The ruler strip follows the page's list; its entries overlap around 1260-1290 and the page does not resolve them. The lands of Yaroslavl are inside Cliopatria's Rostov-Suzdal row to 1240 and Vladimir-Suzdal from 1294 (overlap to be carved by the renderer). Wikidata id unknown. Repair of 2026-11-01 (review finding): the region is now the Yaroslavl oblast, Lake Kubenskoye and the Sheksna less 40 km round Rostov Veliky, 30 km round Uglich and 30 km round Pereslavl-Zalessky, because those towns were the seats of the principalities of Rostov (absorbed 1474), Uglich (1218-1328, then Moscow, then Andrey Bolshoy's appanage from 1462) and Pereslavl (1175-1302, then Moscow); three pages were added (Pereslavl-Zalessky, Uglich, Ivan III), five pages in all. Rostov and Uglich still have no dossier of their own: Rostov's English title redirects to Vladimir-Suzdal and Uglich's is the town article, so a gap-filler must decide whether their lands (the discs cut out here) are written as principalities or added to the Moscow dossier.
